title: Most Events, One Per Day
statement:
You get a list events, where events[i] = [start, end] means event i is open on every day from start to end, inclusive.

Showing up on any single day inside that range counts as attending the event. You can attend at most one event per day, and each event counts once.

Return the largest number of events you can attend.

examples.why: Taking [1, 5] on day 1 just because it starts first would lose [1, 1]. Spend day 1 on [1, 1], day 2 on [2, 2], and any later day on [1, 5].
Three events share only days 1 and 2, so one of them is lost. [3, 3] still gets day 3.

hints: Go day by day. On a given day, several open events may be waiting. Which one should you attend?
Attend the open event that closes soonest. Any other choice can only leave you with a more urgent event and fewer days for it.
Sort events by start. Walk the days; push the end day of every event that starts today into a min-heap, drop ends that already passed, then attend the event at the top of the heap.

explain.intuition:
On any day, the question is which open event to spend the day on. The one that closes soonest is always a safe pick. Suppose an optimal plan attends some other event today and the soonest-closing one on a later day (or never). Swapping them keeps the plan valid, because the other event stays open at least as long. So the greedy choice never hurts.

To find the soonest-closing open event quickly, keep a min-heap of end days. Events enter the heap on their start day, expired ones are dropped from the top, and each day you pop one. It works like a task queue sorted by deadline.
steps: Sort events by start day. Keep an index i into the sorted list and an empty min-heap of end days.
Let day run forward. If the heap is empty, jump day to the next event's start.
Push the end of every event with start === day and move i forward.
Pop ends smaller than day: those events are over. If something is left, pop it and count one attended event.
Move to day + 1 and repeat until both the list and the heap are empty.
pitfalls: Choosing by earliest start, or attending each event on its first day. Example 2 shows a long event stealing day 1 from a one-day event.
Sorting by end and greedily giving each event its start day. Two events with the same start then fight for one day even when later days are free.
Looping over every day up to the maximum even when the heap is empty and no event starts soon. Jump ahead to the next start instead (or accept the bounded day range).

solutions.title: Scan all events every day
solutions.idea: For each day, look through every unattended event that is open and attend the one that ends first.
solutions.time: O(D × n), D = last end day

solutions.title: Sweep days with a min-heap of end days
solutions.idea: Sort by start. Each day, add events that open today, discard expired ones, and attend the open event that ends first.

solutions.title: Sort by end, take the earliest free day
solutions.idea: Handle events in order of end day and give each the earliest free day at or after its start. A union-find 'next free day' pointer finds that day in near-constant time.

followups: Each event now has a value, and you can attend at most k events in total, each over its whole range. How does the problem change? (Hint: DP + binary search.)
Return which day you attend each event, not just the count.
lcTitle: Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended
